description: These proteins share residence in or passage through the Golgi membrane, the sorting and modification hub where newly made proteins and lipids are glycosylated, remodelled and dispatched to their destinations. The grouping links glycan synthesis to lipid metabolism and cargo sorting: B3GNT5 extends glycosphingolipid chains, CSGALNACT1 initiates chondroitin sulfate chains on proteoglycan core proteins, and SGMS2 makes sphingomyelin from ceramide in the trans-Golgi, supplying the lipid that structures the secretory pathway and the plasma membrane. SORT1 acts as a sorting receptor that routes cargo between Golgi, endosomes and the cell surface, while WLS is the dedicated carrier that loads lipid-modified Wnt ligands for secretion, so Wnt-dependent patterning fails without it. Growth factor and receptor cargo such as PDGFC and TLR8 traverse the same compartment, illustrating how Golgi transit determines what a cell ultimately secretes or displays.

Small GTPase mediated signal transduction converts receptor engagement into changes in the actin cytoskeleton, cell shape, adhesion and motility, and the genes here represent the haematopoietic arm of that control. Rho-family switches such as RAC2 and RHOG are loaded with GTP by exchange factors including VAV1 and FGD3, which couple immune receptor and kinase signalling to cytoskeletal remodelling. The set is dominated by the off switches and brakes: a large family of Rho GTPase-activating proteins that stimulate GTP hydrolysis, and guanine nucleotide dissociation inhibitors that sequester inactive GTPases in the cytosol. RHOH is atypical, lacking GTPase activity and acting instead as a constitutively GTP-bound adaptor. The balance of activators and inactivators sets how transiently and how locally a GTPase is switched on, which is what allows leukocytes to polarise, migrate and rearrange their cortex on demand.

Cell proliferation depends on an ordered progression through the mitotic cell cycle — G1, S, G2 and M — in which the genome is replicated once and then partitioned equally into two daughter cells. The programme is driven by cyclin-dependent kinases paired with successive cyclins, restrained by CDK inhibitors such as p21 and p27 and by the retinoblastoma–E2F switch that licenses S-phase entry, and reset by ubiquitin-mediated destruction of cyclins and securin through the anaphase-promoting complex and SCF ligases. Origin licensing by MCM proteins, checkpoint kinases responding to DNA damage or replication stress, kinetochore and spindle assembly checkpoint components, condensin and cohesin, centrosomal and microtubule machinery, and ESCRT-dependent abscission at the cleavage furrow each govern a distinct step. Loss of these controls produces aneuploidy, genome instability and unchecked growth, which is why the pathway is central to cancer and to development.

When a T cell meets antigen presented on MHC together with costimulation, it changes shape, upregulates activation markers, proliferates and commits to an effector programme; this is the step that converts specific recognition into an actual immune response. The genes here span the antigen-presentation and costimulatory interface (HLA class II, CD74, CD80/CD86, ICOS and its ligand, ICAM1 and the integrin LFA-1), the cytokine and JAK-STAT circuitry that instructs lineage choice, and the transcription factors that define the resulting subsets — TBX21 for Th1, GATA3 for Th2, RORC for Th17, BCL6 for follicular helper and FOXP3 for regulatory T cells. Immunoproteasome subunits, IL-12/IL-23/IL-6 receptor components and negative regulators such as SOCS3, SMAD7 and the roquin proteins set the threshold and duration of the response. Too little yields immunodeficiency; unchecked activation drives autoimmunity and chronic inflammation.

A T cell commits to an immune response only when its receptor engages antigen displayed on an MHC molecule by an antigen-presenting cell, and this pathway covers the cell-cell contact that turns that recognition into changed morphology and behaviour. It is the decision point for adaptive immunity: too little and infection or tumour escapes, too much and autoimmunity follows. Adhesion and stabilisation of the immunological synapse come from the LFA-1 integrin subunit ITGAL with its ligand ICAM1 and the adaptor APBB1IP, which couples inside-out integrin activation. Antigen loading onto class II molecules depends on the HLA-DM chain. Much of the remainder is restraint: HAVCR2 with galectin-9, LILRB1, and FGL2 dampen or terminate activation, while semaphorin-plexin and TREM2-TYROBP signalling further tune the interaction. The balance of adhesive and inhibitory inputs sets the threshold and duration of T cell priming.

Processes that raise the frequency, rate or extent of T cell mediated immunity are gathered here: the events that make antigen visible to T cells and then push responding cells toward effector differentiation. Antigen presentation supplies the front end, with classical class I and class II molecules plus beta-2 microglobulin and a peptide transporter, alongside the lipid-presenting CD1 family and the metabolite-presenting MR1 that serve unconventional T cell subsets. Stress-induced ULBP and RAET1 ligands and nectin-family surface proteins engage activating receptors on cytotoxic lymphocytes, while costimulation and adhesion are contributed by molecules such as CD81, SLAMF1 and OX40 ligand. Cytokines and their receptors — IL-12, IL-18, IL-23, IL-1beta, IL-4, IL-6 — act with the transcription factors TBX21, GATA3 and FOXP3 to specify helper and regulatory fates, and adaptors including MALT1, TRAF2, TRAF6 and MAP3K7 relay the receptor signals inward.

Systemic arterial blood pressure is set moment to moment by circulating and locally released chemical signals acting on vessel tone, cardiac output and renal salt and water handling. This hormonal, autocrine and paracrine control is what keeps perfusion adequate on standing or after blood loss, and its derangement underlies essential hypertension, pre-eclampsia and heart failure. The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis dominates: renin cleaves angiotensinogen, angiotensin-converting enzyme generates angiotensin II for AT1 and AT2 receptors, while ACE2 and a Mas receptor arm oppose it and aldosterone synthase drives mineralocorticoid production. Vasopressin and oxytocin receptors, endothelins with their converting enzyme, adrenergic and dopaminergic receptors, substance P and tachykinin signalling, and thrombin-activated protease receptors add further inputs, balanced against endothelial nitric oxide synthase-derived vasodilation and modulated by NADPH oxidase-generated superoxide and mast cell proteases.

Control over how fast carbohydrates are made, stored and broken down is what lets a body hold blood glucose steady between meals and match fuel use to demand. This regulatory layer sits above glycolysis, gluconeogenesis and glycogen turnover rather than carrying flux itself, and its loss is a route into insulin resistance and disordered glucose handling. Hormonal inputs converge here: insulin and glucagon through their receptors, IRS adaptors, AKT and GSK3, alongside glucocorticoid receptor signalling and adipokines such as leptin and adiponectin. Energy sensing runs in parallel through AMPK subunits, mTOR complex components and sirtuins. Effectors include glucokinase and fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase at committed steps, the pyruvate dehydrogenase kinases that gate pyruvate oxidation, and a family of protein phosphatase 1 glycogen-targeting subunits. Transcriptional regulators including FOXO1, HIF1A, PPARGC1A, MLXIPL and TCF7L2 set longer-term capacity, with several microRNAs tuning the output.

Signals that raise cyclic AMP are terminated by hydrolysing the nucleotide to 5'-AMP, and this catabolic route is how a cell resets after stimulation by hormones and neurotransmitters that act through adenylyl cyclase. The enzymes here are cAMP-specific phosphodiesterases, which cleave the 3',5'-cyclic phosphate and so limit the duration and spatial spread of protein kinase A activation. Individual family members differ in affinity, regulation and localisation: the PDE4 enzymes dominate in inflammatory and immune cells and are the target of drugs used in asthma, COPD and psoriasis, while PDE10A is enriched in striatal neurons and has been pursued in schizophrenia and Huntington disease. PDE7 and PDE8 forms act in lymphocytes and steroidogenic and endocrine tissue. Because cAMP governs secretion, contractility, metabolism and gene transcription, its degradation shapes responsiveness in essentially every tissue.

Before a cell divides it must copy its genome exactly once, and replication initiation is the step that decides where and when copying starts. Origin recognition complex subunits mark origins in G1, CDC6 and CDT1 load the MCM2-7 helicase to license them, and rising cyclin E-CDK2 activity together with CDC45, GINS and TOPBP1/TICRR converts licensed origins into unwound, primed forks where the polymerase alpha-primase complex lays down RNA-DNA primers. Licensing is confined to G1 by geminin, which sequesters CDT1, and by CRL4-DTL-mediated degradation of CDT1 after firing, so that no origin fires twice; loss of this restraint causes re-replication, amplification and genome instability of the kind that drives cancer. The same machinery is redeployed developmentally, as MCIDAS and GMNC direct centriole amplification in multiciliated cells.

Chromatin organization covers how DNA is packaged with histones into nucleosomes and how that packaging is built, moved, marked and dismantled so that genes can be read, replicated and repaired at the right time. It sets which parts of the genome are accessible, underlies cell identity and its inheritance through division, and its failure produces developmental syndromes, imprinting disorders and many cancers. Core and linker histones plus variants such as H2A.Z, macroH2A, H3.3 and the centromeric CENP-A are deposited by chaperones like ASF1, HIRA, NPM1 and CAF-1, then repositioned by ATP-dependent remodellers of the SWI/SNF, ISWI, CHD and INO80/SRCAP families. Writers, erasers and readers of acetylation, methylation, phosphorylation and ubiquitylation control Polycomb and heterochromatin silencing, DNA methylation via DNMTs, TETs and UHRF1, cohesin- and CTCF-based genome folding, and the chromatin response to double-strand breaks.

Ribosomes begin as a single long precursor transcript that must be cleaved, trimmed and chemically modified before its rRNA pieces can fold into working subunits; rRNA processing is that conversion. It supplies the cell with translation capacity, and defects in it cause the ribosomopathies — bone marrow failure and skeletal phenotypes seen with mutations in factors such as SBDS. Most of the work occurs in the nucleolus, where small nucleolar RNA-guided complexes install 2'-O-methyl groups through fibrillarin and pseudouridines through the dyskerin-NHP2-NOP10-GAR1 particle, while methyltransferases and RNA helicases of the DEAD-box family remodel the precursor. Endonucleases and the exosome with its associated exonucleases remove spacer sequences, and small-subunit processome components of the UTP and WDR families organise early cleavages. Ribosomal proteins themselves participate, and parallel enzymes modify mitochondrial rRNA. Nucleolar stress arising here also links ribosome assembly to p53 control of growth.

Newly made proteins have to reach the compartment where they work, and protein targeting is the collection of recognition and delivery steps that gets them there, usually by reading a sorting signal built into the polypeptide. Without it, secretory and membrane proteins never enter the endoplasmic reticulum, mitochondria and peroxisomes cannot import their proteomes, and lysosomal enzymes are secreted instead of stored. The signal recognition particle and its receptor deliver ribosomes to the Sec61 translocon, where signal peptidase removes the cleaved sequence; tail-anchored proteins use a separate insertion route; TOM and TIM translocases with matrix processing peptidases handle mitochondrial precursors; PEX proteins recognise peroxisomal targeting signals; and mannose-6-phosphate tagging routes hydrolases to lysosomes. Palmitoyltransferases, adaptor and retromer-like complexes, ubiquitin ligases and autophagy receptors then position or redirect cargo, linking targeting to organelle quality control and diseases such as peroxisome biogenesis disorders and lysosomal storage.

Endoderm development traces the innermost germ layer from its specification at gastrulation to the mature epithelia that give rise to the gut tube, liver, pancreas, thyroid and lung. Nodal and GDF ligands signalling through SMAD2/3 with SMAD4 drive pluripotent cells into a mesendodermal state, where EOMES, MIXL1 and then SOX17, GATA4/6, HNF1B, ONECUT1 and NKX2-1 progressively commit cells to definitive endoderm and its organ territories, while POU5F1, NANOG and SOX2 mark the pluripotent starting point. BMP4 with BMPR1A, FGF8 and Wnt input via CTNNB1 pattern the emerging sheet, and secreted antagonists tune it: Noggin blocks BMP, DKK1 blocks Wnt. Movement and epithelial remodelling depend on collagens, laminins, fibronectin, integrins and MMP-mediated matrix turnover, and the transcriptional output is shaped by the PAF1 elongation complex, HDAC1, SETD2 and Mediator.

Cardiogenesis takes mesodermal progenitors through specification, looping of the linear heart tube, chamber and valve formation, septation, conduction system patterning and coronary vascularization, ending in a four-chambered pump that contracts rhythmically for life. Failure at any step underlies congenital heart disease, laterality defects and cardiomyopathy. Lineage transcription factors such as NKX2-5, GATA4, TBX5, HAND1/2, MEF2C and ISL1 act with chromatin regulators and Notch, BMP/TGF-beta, Wnt, Hedgehog, FGF and Nodal signalling to assign chamber identity and left-right asymmetry; motile and primary cilia genes set the initial laterality cue. Endocardial cushions form by endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition and remodel through matrix proteins and metalloproteinases into valves, while neural crest and second heart field cells build the outflow tract. Differentiation converges on sarcomere assembly and excitation-contraction coupling components including MYH6, TNNT2, TTN, RYR2 and SCN5A, alongside microRNAs and Hippo-YAP control of cardiomyocyte growth.

Behaviour is the coordinated output of the nervous system — feeding, sleep and circadian timing, locomotion, learning and memory, social interaction, reproduction, nociception and reward — and this broad collection captures the molecules through which those actions are generated and tuned. Neurotransmitter systems dominate: dopamine, serotonin, opioid, glutamate and GABA receptors, transporters such as SLC6A3 and SLC6A4, and synthetic enzymes including TH and GAD1. Neuropeptide circuits for energy balance and arousal are prominent, with POMC, AGRP, NPY, leptin and its receptor, orexins, oxytocin and CRH acting on hypothalamic targets. Synaptic adhesion and scaffolding proteins (neurexins, neuroligins, SHANK family, SYNGAP1), activity-induced transcription factors such as FOS and NPAS4, ion channels and clock components complete the picture. Disruption of these genes underlies autism and intellectual disability, addiction, obesity, sleep disorders and neurodegenerative disease, linking molecular synaptic function to whole-organism conduct.

Sugars cannot cross membranes unaided, so cells depend on dedicated carriers to take up glucose, fructose and related solutes and to move them between tissues. Carbohydrate transport of this kind sets blood glucose, fuels the brain and red cells, allows the intestine and kidney to absorb and reclaim dietary sugar, and fails visibly in diabetes and in inherited glucose transporter deficiencies causing seizures or renal glycosuria. Two carrier families dominate: facilitative GLUT-type uniporters that follow the concentration gradient, and sodium-coupled cotransporters that drive uptake against it, the target of modern glycosuric drugs. Much of the remainder is regulation. Insulin acting through its receptor, IRS adaptors, PI3K and AKT triggers translocation of the storage transporter to the plasma membrane of muscle and fat, with Rab and SNARE-associated trafficking proteins executing the step, while leptin, adiponectin, growth hormone and inflammatory cytokines tune sensitivity. Aquaporin channels contribute glycerol and related permeability.

Wnt signalling tells a cell where it is, what to become, and whether to keep dividing, and it does so from embryonic patterning through to the maintenance of adult stem cells in gut, skin and bone. Secreted Wnt ligands, lipid-modified by porcupine and exported with the help of Wntless, engage Frizzled receptors together with LRP5/6 or alternative receptors such as ROR and RYK. In the canonical branch, receptor engagement disables the destruction complex built on APC, Axin, CK1 and GSK3, so beta-catenin escapes ubiquitin-mediated degradation, enters the nucleus and partners with TCF/LEF and Pygopus/BCL9 to drive targets including MYC and cyclin D1, while Groucho/TLE repressors hold those promoters off in the unstimulated state. Non-canonical arms acting through Dishevelled, Vangl, Prickle and Rho-family GTPases orient cells during planar polarity and convergent extension. Secreted antagonists (DKKs, SFRPs, sclerostin, NOTUM) and the RSPO-LGR-RNF43/ZNRF3 module set signal strength; loss of this control underlies colorectal and other cancers, skeletal disease and developmental malformation.

Leukotrienes are lipid mediators that make blood vessels leak, recruit neutrophils, and constrict airway smooth muscle, so their biosynthesis sets the intensity of acute inflammatory and allergic responses; drugs blocking this route are used in asthma. Phospholipases such as PLA2G4A release arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipids, and 5-lipoxygenase acting with its nuclear membrane partner ALOX5AP converts it to the unstable epoxide leukotriene A4. From there the pathway branches: leukotriene A4 hydrolase yields the chemotactic LTB4, while leukotriene C4 synthase and related membrane-bound glutathione transferases conjugate glutathione to form LTC4. Export by the ABCC1 transporter and successive extracellular trimming by gamma-glutamyl transferases and dipeptidases generate LTD4 and LTE4, the cysteinyl leukotrienes that signal through receptors on airway and vascular tissue. Mast cells, eosinophils and myeloid cells are the principal producers.

Shaping tissues and organs during development requires not only the machinery that builds them but control over how fast and how far that building goes, and this broad regulatory programme covers the modulation of anatomical structure morphogenesis. It governs how epithelia branch, how blood vessels sprout and remodel, how neurons extend and steer axons and dendrites, and how mitochondria and cell shape are reorganized to permit those movements. The effectors are correspondingly varied: Rho-family GTPases with their exchange factors and GAPs acting on the actin cytoskeleton, guidance cues and receptors such as netrins, slits, semaphorins, ephrins and their plexin, Robo and Eph partners, angiogenic ligands including VEGFA and angiopoietins with KDR, TEK and NRP1, and morphogen inputs from WNT, BMP, TGF-beta, FGF and Hedgehog families, layered with transcription factors and microRNAs that tune the response. Misregulation underlies congenital malformations, vascular anomalies and abnormal tissue remodelling in disease.

Pancreatic beta cells release insulin in proportion to blood glucose, and this regulated secretion is what keeps circulating glucose within a narrow range; its failure produces diabetes. Glucose entering through the GLUT2 transporter is phosphorylated by glucokinase, and the resulting rise in ATP closes the KATP channel formed by KCNJ11 and ABCC8, depolarizing the cell and opening voltage-gated calcium entry. Calcium then triggers fusion of insulin granules, in which proinsulin has already been cleaved to mature hormone, using SNARE proteins such as STX1A and SNAP25 together with the calcium sensor SYT7 and Rab-dependent granule trafficking. The output is tuned by incretin and adrenergic receptors acting through cyclic AMP, by somatostatin and dopamine inhibition, by leptin and inflammatory cytokines, and by circadian cues. Transcription factors including PDX1, NKX6-1, MAFA, NEUROD1 and the HNFs establish and maintain the secretory phenotype, and their mutation causes monogenic diabetes.

Nearly every mRNA must be cleaved and polyadenylated at its 3' end before it can be exported and translated, and this pathway covers the factors that stimulate that maturation step, raising its rate or efficiency. Efficient 3'-end formation determines transcript stability, correct termination of transcription, and which polyadenylation site is chosen, so gene output depends on it as much as on initiation. Contributors here act from several directions: the nuclear cap-binding complex, composed of NCBP1 and NCBP2, binds the newly added 5' cap and communicates across the transcript to promote downstream processing events; CDC73, a component of the PAF1 transcription elongation complex, couples events at the elongating polymerase to cleavage and polyadenylation. The set also includes the RNA helicase DHX36 and CCNB1. Defective 3'-end processing leaves unstable, poorly exported transcripts and disrupted transcriptional termination.

Methylation is the covalent transfer of a methyl group, almost always from S-adenosylmethionine, onto DNA, RNA, protein, lipids, and small molecules, and it is one of the broadest ways a cell tunes the function of molecules it has already made. The enzymes here cover that whole range: DNMT1 and DNMT3A/3B mark cytosines in DNA to set heritable gene silencing; histone methyltransferases of the SET, PRDM, EZH, SUV39 and KMT2 families write the marks that define active and repressed chromatin; PRMT arginine methyltransferases modify histones and RNA-binding proteins; METTL3-METTL14 and cap-associated enzymes methylate mRNA adenosines and 5' caps, while large families of tRNA and rRNA modifiers support accurate, efficient translation in cytosol and mitochondria. Others act on metabolites and drugs, on protein carboxyl and N-terminal groups, or on ubiquinone and phospholipid synthesis. Methyl supply itself is regulated, via homocysteine remethylation and mitochondrial SAM import, linking this chemistry to one-carbon metabolism.

Interferon-gamma drives macrophage activation and Th1 immunity, and this pathway covers the processes that damp its production, keeping that arm of inflammation in check once it is no longer needed. Restraint is imposed at several levels: inhibitory surface receptors and their ligands on T and NK cells, including PD-L1, PD-L2, TIM-3 with its galectin-9 ligand, VISTA and LILRB family receptors; suppressive cytokines such as IL-10 and the IL-33/ST2 and IL-20 receptor systems; transcriptional regulators including FOXP3, which specifies regulatory T cells, and GATA3, which favours a Th2 program over interferon-gamma-producing Th1 cells. Post-transcriptional control appears through the ribonuclease ZC3H12A and microRNAs, alongside TGF-beta family members and innate sensors such as NLRP6 and TLR4. The collected activities link antigen-presenting cell signalling, T cell co-inhibition and cytokine feedback to the control of type II interferon output.

Myeloid cells such as neutrophils, monocytes and macrophages are short-lived by design, and signals that increase their rate of programmed cell death set how quickly an inflammatory response is terminated. Promoting myeloid apoptosis clears spent granulocytes from inflamed tissue so that macrophages can engulf them without spilling proteases and oxidants, and it limits the size of the myeloid compartment produced by the marrow; when this control fails, neutrophils persist and inflammation becomes chronic, while excessive death contributes to neutropenia. The genes here act at several levels: annexin A1 is a glucocorticoid-inducible mediator of neutrophil apoptosis and its safe removal, HCAR2 and ADIPOQ transmit metabolic and adipokine cues to myeloid cells, CDKN2A links the tumour suppressor axis to death sensitivity, SIRT1 and MEF2C shape transcriptional survival programmes, and class I phosphoinositide 3-kinase catalytic subunits set the survival signalling that this process must overcome.

Steroid hormones act through intracellular receptors that bind DNA and change transcription, and this pathway covers the braking mechanisms that damp, terminate or prevent that output. Without such restraint, oestrogen, androgen, glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid signalling runs unopposed, a situation linked to hormone-driven breast and prostate cancers and to disordered stress and metabolic responses. Repression works at several levels: corepressors NCOR1 and NCOR2 recruit histone deacetylase activity to receptor-bound promoters, SIRT1 and HDAC1 remove activating acetyl marks, SMARCA4 alters chromatin access, and NR0B1 (DAX1) blocks receptor transactivation directly. CRY1 and CRY2 repress glucocorticoid receptor activity, while PIAS2 modifies receptors by SUMOylation and CCR4-NOT subunits act as transcriptional corepressors. Others limit ligand availability or receptor trafficking. The collective effect is to set the gain and duration of hormone responses in target tissues rather than to switch them on.

Ion fluxes across membranes must be damped as well as driven, and this collection covers the braking mechanisms: processes that reduce the rate or extent of ion movement through channels, pumps and exchangers. Such restraint sets the duration of action potentials, limits calcium loading, and protects cells from the energetic and osmotic cost of unchecked flux. Several routes are represented. Accessory subunits such as the KCNE proteins modify the gating of partners including KCNQ1 and KCNH2, setting cardiac repolarisation; sarcolipin and phospholamban inhibit the sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium pump to tune contractility; calmodulin with calcineurin subunits provides calcium-dependent feedback; NEDD4 and NEDD4L ubiquitin ligases remove transporters from the surface; MCUB blunts mitochondrial calcium uptake. Numerous microRNAs add post-transcriptional suppression of channel expression. Loss of such control contributes to arrhythmia, hypertension and excitotoxic injury.</description>Ta**Homework Project – Advanced Calculus Applications** (Unit 4) Students must show all reasoning.
