Helper T cells only act after they see peptide presented on MHC class II, and CD4-positive, alpha-beta T cell activation is the transition from a resting naive cell to a proliferating, cytokine-secreting effector. It underwrites nearly all adaptive immunity, licensing B cell antibody responses and macrophage killing, while its miscalibration produces autoimmunity, allergy, or, when blunted, susceptibility to intracellular pathogens. Antigen recognition through class II molecules such as HLA-DRA and HLA-DRB1 is reinforced by costimulation from CD80, CD86, ICOS and OX40 ligand, and restrained by checkpoint ligands including PD-L1 and VISTA; signals converge on PKC-theta, MALT1 and NF-kB, mTOR, and JAK1/JAK3-STAT modules driven by IL-2, IL-6, IL-12, IL-21 and IL-23. Lineage-defining transcription factors -- TBX21, GATA3, RORC, BCL6, FOXP3 and ZBTB7B -- then fix the helper subset, with SOCS proteins, the RC3H ubiquitin ligases and proteasome subunits limiting the response.

The intestinal epithelium renews itself every few days, and that depends on keeping the number of crypt-base stem cells steady — enough to replenish absorptive and secretory lineages, not so many that crypts expand into adenomas. Intestinal stem cell homeostasis is the set of processes that holds this balance. LGR4 is a receptor for R-spondins and potentiates Wnt signalling in the crypt, the central input sustaining the stem cell compartment; loss of Wnt output collapses crypt proliferation, while excess drives hyperplasia. Lipid handling contributes as well, with LPCAT3 remodelling membrane phospholipids and secreted phospholipases altering the crypt lipid environment, and PLA2G2A is a Paneth cell product with antibacterial activity. NOD2 links bacterial peptidoglycan sensing to stem cell survival, connecting this niche to the microbiota and to Crohn's disease susceptibility. ZNHIT1 supplies chromatin regulation through H2A.Z deposition.

Presynaptic terminals must reuse their vesicle membrane to sustain transmitter release, and one route does so indirectly: vesicles retrieved from the plasma membrane through clathrin-coated pits are delivered into an endosomal compartment before new synaptic vesicles are regenerated from it, re-acidified and refilled with neurotransmitter. Routing through an endosomal intermediate allows sorting and quality control of vesicle proteins that direct budding back from the membrane cannot provide. The components reflect this dual identity: intersectins couple endocytic coat machinery to actin and small GTPase regulation at the site of retrieval, an adaptor complex subunit shared with lysosome-related organelle biogenesis selects cargo for budding from endosomes, GRIPAP1 acts as a scaffold on neuronal recycling endosomes, and RAB7A marks the late endosomal step. The pathway thus sits at the intersection of membrane traffic, organelle identity and the replenishment of releasable vesicle pools.

Locomotion covers the self-propelled movement of cells and whole organisms from one place to another, and in humans it is mostly cell migration: leukocytes crossing vessel walls to reach infection, endothelial tips sprouting new vessels, neural crest and axonal growth cones navigating the embryo, keratinocytes closing a wound, and sperm swimming. Its failure leaves immunodeficiency, defective vascular and neural patterning and poor healing, while its inappropriate reactivation underlies tumour invasion and metastasis. The genes span the layers this requires: chemokines and their receptors, growth factor and semaphorin/slit/ephrin guidance cues, integrins, cadherins and matrix components that provide traction, metalloproteinases that clear a path, and Rho-family GTPases with their regulators, actin nucleators, cofilin, profilin and myosin light-chain kinase that build and retract the leading edge. Ciliary and flagellar components add motile cilia and sperm propulsion, and numerous microRNAs and transcription factors tune the whole programme.

Cocaine blocks monoamine reuptake, and the cellular and behavioural changes that follow constitute the response to cocaine: acute reward, sensitization with repeated exposure, and the lasting plasticity that underlies addiction and relapse. The dopamine transporter targeted by the drug is here alongside serotonin transport, catechol-O-methyltransferase-mediated dopamine breakdown, and the full set of D1- through D5-class dopamine receptors that transduce the resulting surge in striatal projection neurons, where DARPP-32 and CDK5 integrate the signal. Glutamatergic components -- AMPA receptor subunits, Homer scaffolds and astrocytic glutamate transporters -- account for synaptic remodelling in reward circuitry. Stable transcriptional adaptation is imposed through CREB, accumulating FosB, DNA methyltransferase and histone deacetylase activity. Stress and neuropeptide elements, including corticotropin-releasing hormone with its binding protein, oxytocin, CART, nociceptin and the kappa-opioid receptor, connect drug exposure to negative affect and stress-driven craving.

During gastrulation, cells of the early embryo must decide whether to become mesoderm, the germ layer that gives rise to heart, blood, muscle, bone and kidney. This pathway covers the inputs that tune how strongly and how widely that decision is made. Positive signals come from WNT3A acting through canonical Wnt signalling, from fibroblast growth factor reception via FGFR1, and from bone morphogenetic protein signalling through the type I receptor BMPR1A; each feeds into the transcriptional programme that commits epiblast cells to a mesodermal identity, with MESP1 acting as a key transcription factor downstream in nascent mesoderm. Restraint comes from secreted antagonists: DKK1 blocks Wnt co-receptor engagement and SFRP2 sequesters Wnt ligands. The balance between these inducers and inhibitors sets the timing, position and amount of mesoderm formed, linking extracellular morphogen gradients to germ layer patterning.

Penile erection is the vascular and smooth-muscle response that permits copulation: arterial inflow into the corpus cavernosum rises while venous outflow is restricted, so the erectile tissue engorges, stiffens and becomes erect. It is a neurovascular reflex integrating central arousal signals with local control of cavernosal smooth muscle tone, and its failure produces erectile dysfunction, a common consequence of diabetic and atherosclerotic vascular disease and of autonomic nerve injury. The genes here point to that mixture of inputs: oxytocin acts as a central and spinal pro-erectile neuropeptide, endothelin receptor signalling and purinergic P2Y1 receptor activation on endothelium and smooth muscle set vasoconstrictor and vasodilator balance, and adenosine deaminase shapes the pool of adenosine acting as a local relaxant. The process links autonomic signalling, endothelial function and reproductive physiology.

Helper T cell fate is as much a matter of restraint as of instruction, and this pathway covers the brakes applied to CD4-positive alpha-beta T cell differentiation. Limiting how readily naive CD4 cells commit, and blocking entry into the wrong effector programme, keeps the balance between Th1, Th2, Th17 and regulatory outputs appropriate to an infection and prevents autoimmune or allergic pathology. The machinery is largely transcriptional and post-transcriptional: RUNX1 and RUNX3 with their CBFB partner, BCL6, the CD4/CD8 lineage factor ZBTB7B, and FOXP3, which enforces a regulatory rather than conventional effector identity; TBX21 commits toward Th1 while excluding alternatives. Cytokine signalling is dampened by SOCS5 and by SMAD7 acting on TGF-beta responses, while the RNA-binding proteins RC3H1, RC3H2 and ZC3H12A degrade transcripts encoding costimulatory and cytokine drivers, and galectin-1 and annexin A1 impose extrinsic limits.

Pigmentation covers how melanin and related pigments accumulate in skin, hair, eyes and inner ear, whether by making more pigment per cell or by generating more pigment cells. It determines visible colour, shields keratinocyte DNA from ultraviolet damage, and supports retinal and cochlear function; its failure gives albinism, Waardenburg and Hermansky-Pudlak syndromes, piebaldism and hearing loss, while dysregulated melanocyte growth underlies melanoma. Melanoblasts arise from neural crest under MITF, SOX10 and KIT signalling, then build melanosomes as lysosome-related organelles: tyrosinase and TYRP1 catalyse melanin synthesis, PMEL forms the internal matrix, and OCA2 and SLC45A2 set organelle pH and ion balance. Adaptor and biogenesis complexes together with Rab GTPases deliver cargo to maturing melanosomes, and myosin Va with RAB27A and melanophilin captures them for transfer to neighbouring cells. Melanocortin receptor signalling opposed by agouti protein tunes the pigment type produced.

The sensory epithelium of the cochlea contains a precise mosaic of mechanosensory hair cells separated by supporting cells, and this pathway sets how many progenitors take the auditory receptor cell fate and when. ATOH1 is the proneural transcription factor required for hair cell differentiation, while Notch-mediated lateral inhibition restrains it: DLL1 presented by nascent hair cells activates NOTCH1 in neighbours, inducing the HES and HEY repressors that block the hair cell programme and direct those cells toward supporting-cell identity. MYCN and MYCL contribute proliferative control in the developing otic epithelium, coupling progenitor expansion to the timing of differentiation, and ESRP1 acts through epithelial splicing regulation. The output is the correct number and spacing of hair cells, which determines hearing sensitivity; altered dosage of these regulators shifts the balance between receptor and supporting cell fates.

Cells build fatty acids for membranes, energy storage and signalling, and this pathway covers the inputs that turn that biosynthetic output up rather than the synthetic steps themselves. Stimulation comes from several directions: nuclear receptors and transcription factors including the liver X receptors NR1H2 and NR1H3 and the carbohydrate-responsive factor MLXIPL couple nutrient and sterol status to lipogenic gene expression, while MID1IP1 acts on acetyl-CoA carboxylase activity and the acetyltransferase KAT2B and deacetylase SIRT2 place the process under acetylation control. Microbial and inflammatory mediators such as IL1B, PTGS2 and the endothelins tie lipid synthesis to inflammatory and vascular signalling, and hormonal input arrives through vasopressin and its receptor. Elongation and remodelling enzymes, peroxisomal fatty acid transporters, and apolipoproteins that govern lipoprotein lipase activity place the regulation in the wider context of lipid flux between tissues.

Paraxial mesoderm morphogenesis shapes the bands of mesoderm flanking the neural tube into organized presomitic tissue and somites, the source of the axial skeleton, skeletal muscle and dermis. Getting this geometry right determines vertebral segmentation and body-wall patterning; failure produces fused or missing vertebrae, rib defects and abnormal muscle and dermal derivatives. The genes here point to two inputs acting on the same tissue: Wnt ligands including WNT3A, WNT5A and WNT11 acting through LEF1-dependent transcription to sustain and pattern the presomitic mesoderm, and TGF-beta/Nodal-family signalling relayed by SMAD2 and SMAD3, alongside the BMP receptor BMPR1A. The forkhead factors FOXC1 and FOXC2 act largely redundantly downstream to specify sclerotome and somite boundaries. Cytoskeletal and vesicle-trafficking components such as NCKAP1 and EXOC4 supply the cell-shape changes and polarized membrane delivery that convert signalling into tissue architecture.

Sour taste is how an animal detects acids, allowing it to reject spoiled or unripe food and to sense the acidity of what it swallows; it is one of the five basic taste qualities carried from the tongue to the brainstem. The genes here encode candidate acid sensors in taste tissue: PKD2L1 and PKD1L3, polycystin-family cation channels, together with acid-sensing ion channels of the degenerin family (ASIC1, ASIC2, ASIC3) and the subunits of the epithelial sodium channel. PKD2L1 in particular labels a subset of taste receptor cells that respond to sour stimuli. Mechanistically, protons acting on or through such channels depolarize the receptor cell, triggering transmitter release onto gustatory afferents and thereby conveying acid detection into perception. The same channel families contribute to salt sensing and to acid sensitivity in neurons elsewhere, placing this pathway within broader chemosensory signalling.

Smooth muscle cells are not permanently fixed in their contractile state: they can be held in, or returned to, a proliferative, synthetic, dedifferentiated phenotype, and the processes that negatively regulate smooth muscle cell differentiation do exactly that. This restraint matters during vessel development and wound repair, and its persistence underlies intimal thickening, restenosis after angioplasty and the fibroproliferative lesions of atherosclerosis. Growth factors such as PDGFB and FGF9 and the EGF-family ligand EREG drive cells away from the contractile programme; Notch effectors HEY1 and HEY2 and the transcriptional repressor PRDM6 suppress contractile gene expression; DNA methylation and methyl-CpG reading by DNMT1 and MECP2 add epigenetic silencing. Calcineurin-NFAT signalling, tuned by its inhibitor RCAN1, and a set of microRNAs including miR-21, miR-221 and miR-143/145-adjacent regulators tip the balance between proliferation and maturation.

Chromosomes segregate accurately only if each kinetochore is captured by microtubules from the correct spindle pole, and this pathway governs how strongly and how selectively those attachments form. Its output feeds the spindle assembly checkpoint: erroneous or tensionless connections are detached and the cell held in mitosis until they are corrected, so loss of control produces lagging chromosomes, aneuploidy and the chromosomal instability typical of tumours. The chromosomal passenger complex — Aurora B kinase with INCENP, survivin and borealin — phosphorylates outer kinetochore substrates to destabilise improper attachments, while CDK1–cyclin B sets mitotic timing and NEK2 acts at centrosomes and kinetochores. Checkpoint and attachment components such as ZW10, ZWILCH, KNTC1 and the astrin partner KNSTRN report or stabilise the microtubule interface, and acetyltransferase and sirtuin activities tune the process.

Most of the skeleton is made twice: a cartilage model is laid down first and then replaced by bone, and endochondral bone morphogenesis is that conversion. It sets limb and vertebral length, drives postnatal growth at the physis, and its disruption produces chondrodysplasias, short stature and defective fracture healing. Chondrocytes commit under SOX9 and secrete a matrix of collagen II, matrilin and cartilage oligomeric matrix protein; proliferation and the pace of hypertrophy are timed by Indian hedgehog, CNP signalling through its guanylyl cyclase receptor NPR2, and FGF18 acting on FGFR3. Hypertrophic cells then mineralize with the help of alkaline phosphatase, invite vascular and osteoclast invasion, and matrix metalloproteinases clear the cartilage scaffold while RUNX2-dependent osteoblasts deposit collagen I bone. BMP and TGF-beta receptors, retinoic acid receptors and ciliary transport components tune each transition.

The submandibular salivary gland is built by branching morphogenesis, and the epithelial cell proliferation that drives it supplies the cells that elongate and repeatedly divide the epithelial bud into the secretory and ductal tree of the mature gland. Growth is instructed by the surrounding mesenchyme: FGF10 secreted by mesenchymal cells acts on epithelial FGFR2 to sustain proliferation at the bud tips, and loss of this ligand-receptor pair arrests glandular development at an early stage. Hedgehog signalling through SHH provides a further epithelial-mesenchymal cue, and transcriptional regulators are also represented, linking the proliferative response to a shape change rather than to undirected expansion. The same logic of reciprocal signalling operates in other branched exocrine organs, so this biology sits within the broader programme of epithelial branching and organ size control during development.

Coronary vasculature morphogenesis is the process that builds and patterns the heart's own blood supply, converting scattered endothelial and progenitor cells into a hierarchical network of arteries, capillaries and veins that perfuses the myocardium as the wall thickens beyond the reach of diffusion. It depends on signals passing between myocardium, epicardium and the forming vessels: VEGFA acting through the co-receptor NRP1 and FGF2 drive endothelial growth and sprouting, NOTCH1 with the target HEY2 specifies arterial identity, PDGFRB recruits mural cells to stabilize nascent tubes, and TGF-beta receptors including TGFBR1 and the co-receptor TGFBR3 mediate epicardium-derived contributions to vessel walls. Transcriptional regulators such as HAND2, TBX5, TBX1 and the chromatin factor ARID2 set the myocardial and progenitor context in which these cues are interpreted, linking coronary patterning to overall cardiac chamber and vessel development.

Sister chromatids must stay glued together at their centromeres from replication until anaphase, and centromeric sister chromatid cohesion is the process that keeps them so. It matters because premature loss of centromeric cohesion produces unequal chromosome segregation, aneuploid daughter cells and, in oocytes, the chromosome missegregation behind trisomy and age-related infertility. The shugoshin proteins SGO1 and SGO2 mark the inner centromere and recruit a PP2A phosphatase holoenzyme, whose scaffolding subunits PPP2R1A and PPP2R1B appear here, to keep the cohesin ring dephosphorylated and protected from cleavage. The kinase BUB1 phosphorylates centromeric histone H2A to place shugoshin there, linking cohesion protection to the spindle assembly checkpoint and kinetochore geometry; MEIKIN adapts the system for the stepwise, two-division cohesion loss of meiosis. N-terminal acetylation by NAA10/NAA50 and the accessory factor BOD1 tune the same centromeric machinery.

Pituitary follicle-stimulating hormone acts on gonadal target cells, and this is the set of changes those cells make once the hormone is bound: altered gene expression, steroidogenic capacity, growth and secretion. In the ovary it drives granulosa cell proliferation and follicle maturation toward ovulation; in the testis it supports Sertoli cell function and spermatogenesis. Loss of the receptor FSHR causes hypergonadotropic ovarian failure and infertility, placing this response at the centre of reproductive endocrinology. Downstream effects seen here span several arms: endothelin signalling through EDN1 and its receptor EDNRA, TGF-beta family output via the activin/inhibin subunit INHBA, Notch and ephrin-mediated cell contact cues, and induction of glutathione synthesis through GCLC and GCLM, which buffers the oxidative load of steroid hydroxylation supported by the electron donor POR.

Secreted signalling molecules only act where they are allowed to accumulate, and this pathway covers the processes that hold a protein at a defined site in the extracellular region rather than letting it diffuse away. The genes describe two linked strategies. Extracellular matrix components — the fibrillins FBN1 and FBN2 together with latent TGF-beta binding protein LTBP1 — build microfibrils that tether latent TGF-beta family growth factors within the matrix, creating a local reservoir that can be released on demand. Secreted antagonists of the DAN family, including CER1, DAND5 and NBL1, bind BMP and Nodal ligands and restrict their range of action, while NRROS associates with latent TGF-beta1 to control where it is presented. Together these interactions convert diffusible morphogens into spatially bounded signals, shaping gradients during embryonic patterning and constraining growth factor activity in connective tissue.

Programmed cell death of macrophages sets the size and lifespan of tissue phagocyte populations and determines whether an inflammatory lesion resolves or persists. Because macrophages are long-lived sentinels that ingest pathogens and debris, their survival must be tuned to the signals they encounter: infection, cholesterol loading, and cytokine withdrawal all push them toward apoptosis, and in atherosclerotic plaques macrophage death drives necrotic core formation. The genes here connect innate immune sensing to that decision, including a bacterial peptidoglycan sensor, interferon-regulatory transcription factors downstream of nucleic acid sensing, and a chemokine-receptor pair that supports survival. Others act as brakes or accelerators: a NAD-dependent deacetylase and a cell cycle inhibitor of the CDKN2A locus, a lysosomal protease whose release permeabilizes membranes, an ER-resident selenoprotein guarding against ER stress, and a microRNA restraining inflammatory output.

Formation of the distal convoluted tubule shapes the nephron segment that lies just downstream of the loop of Henle and the macula densa, and that reabsorbs a few percent of filtered sodium through the thiazide-sensitive Na-Cl symporter while handling calcium and magnesium transport. Getting this segment built is part of nephron patterning: the paired-box factors PAX2 and PAX8 and the POU-domain factor POU3F3 (BRN1) act in the developing renal epithelium to specify and elongate tubular segments, so that a continuous nephron with distinct proximal, loop and distal identities emerges from the intermediate mesoderm-derived renal vesicle. Segment maturation is marked by the appearance of characteristic products, including the calcium-binding protein calbindin 1 in distal cells and uromodulin in the adjacent thick ascending limb, which together identify where the distal tubule begins and ends.

Bone resorption is carried out by giant multinucleated cells, and osteoclast fusion is the step that makes them: mononuclear osteoclast precursors merge their plasma membranes to form a single multinuclear cell able to seal onto bone and dissolve mineral and matrix. Without this membrane fusion step, precursors remain mononuclear and resorptive capacity is limited, so bone remodelling and skeletal turnover depend on it. Dedicated transmembrane proteins mediate the recognition and merger of apposed cells, with DCSTAMP required for the fusion event itself and the tetraspanin CD81 contributing to membrane organisation at contact sites; SH3PXD2A links the process to actin-based membrane protrusions, and SBNO2 acts as a transcriptional regulator of the fusion programme. The pathway sits at the junction of cell-cell fusion, cytoskeletal remodelling and terminal differentiation of a macrophage-lineage cell.

Heart rate is set by how fast pacemaker cells depolarize and how quickly that excitation spreads through the myocardium, and this is the machinery that tunes both. Its output determines resting and exercising heart rate, the regularity of the beat, and the coordination of atrial and ventricular contraction. Hyperpolarization-activated channels of the HCN family generate the pacemaker current in sinoatrial cells, while voltage-gated calcium and sodium channels with their accessory beta and alpha-2-delta subunits shape the upstroke, and potassium channels including KCNQ1 with KCNE subunits, KCNH2 and inward-rectifiers set repolarization and diastolic potential. Gap junction connexins and desmosomal proteins such as PKP2, DSP and JUP provide the electrical and mechanical coupling that propagation requires, and scaffolding and kinase components including ANK2, AKAP9 and CAMK2D localize and modulate the channels, allowing autonomic and calcium-dependent control of rate.

Before a cell divides, every chromosome must be pulled to the spindle equator so that sister chromatids are under balanced tension and can be split evenly; this pathway comprises the influences that tune how fast and how completely that metaphase plate congression occurs. Failure produces misaligned chromosomes, lagging chromatids and aneuploidy, and the machinery involved is a recurring target in cancer. Central to it is the chromosomal passenger complex — Aurora B with INCENP, survivin and borealin — which corrects improperly attached kinetochores, alongside CDK1 as the mitotic master kinase and the checkpoint protein MAD1L1, which delays anaphase while alignment is incomplete. Spindle organisation and force generation contribute through NUMA1 and cytoplasmic dynein, while SPAG5 supports kinetochore–microtubule attachment. Acetyltransferase and deacetylase activities are also represented, linking chromatin modification to the fidelity of chromosome alignment.

Excitatory synapses work only if NMDA-type glutamate receptors are concentrated at the right patch of postsynaptic membrane rather than dispersed across the neuronal surface, and this clustering process is what puts them there and holds them in place. The result is a postsynaptic density capable of coincidence detection, calcium influx and the plasticity that underlies learning and memory; a synapse whose receptors are not clustered transmits weakly and cannot be potentiated. Trans-synaptic adhesion between neurexin and neuroligin aligns the presynaptic release site with the postsynaptic specialization, while SHANK3 provides the scaffold that links receptor complexes to the actin cytoskeleton. Secreted cues, including reelin acting on neuronal surface receptors and APOE-associated lipoprotein signalling, modulate where and how strongly receptors accumulate, connecting receptor positioning to cortical wiring and synapse maturation.

Every heartbeat begins with a cardiac action potential, and this regulatory biology sets its shape, duration, and how often it fires. It tunes the depolarizing and repolarizing currents that determine conduction through the atria, ventricles, and pacemaking tissue, and thereby the rhythm and coordination of contraction. Voltage-gated and ligand-modulated channels supply the currents: an L-type calcium channel carries the plateau, hyperpolarization-activated HCN channels drive spontaneous pacemaker depolarization, a gap junction connexin propagates excitation between cells, and a calcium-activated TRPM4 channel shapes late repolarization. Their activity is scaled by calmodulin, CaMKII signalling, and scaffolds such as AKAP9, ankyrin-B, and caveolins that place channels at the correct membrane domain. Calcium handling by the ryanodine receptor and the SERCA pump, and desmosomal junction proteins holding myocytes mechanically and electrically coupled, feed back on excitability. Disturbed regulation produces arrhythmia and abnormal conduction.

Removal of the 5' cap commits an mRNA to destruction, and RNA decapping is the step that makes cytoplasmic mRNA turnover irreversible. Once the cap is cleaved, the body of the message is exposed to 5'-to-3' degradation by XRN1, so decapping sets how long a transcript survives and how quickly a cell can change its protein output. The core hydrolase DCP2 works with DCP1A/DCP1B and enhancers such as EDC3, EDC4, PATL1, the LSM1-7 ring and the helicase DDX6, which couples deadenylation by CCR4-NOT and PAN3 to cap loss; ZFP36 delivers AU-rich cytokine mRNAs into this route. A scavenger enzyme, DCPS, clears the leftover cap dinucleotide, while related Nudix hydrolases and DXO act on other capped or aberrantly capped RNAs. The machinery assembles in cytoplasmic granules and links translational repression to decay.

Cytosolic double-stranded DNA, whether from bacteria, viruses or damaged host nuclei, is sensed by AIM2, which oligomerizes with ASC and caspase-1 to drive IL-1β and IL-18 maturation and pyroptotic death. Controlling how readily that platform forms sets the threshold between useful antimicrobial alarm and damaging inflammation, and this regulation shapes host defence against intracellular pathogens as well as susceptibility to autoinflammatory tissue injury. Interferon-inducible guanylate-binding proteins such as GBP2 and GBP5 act upstream by attacking pathogen-containing vacuoles and bacterial surfaces so that DNA becomes accessible to the sensor, effectively licensing assembly. Restraint comes from other quarters: the related DNA sensor IFI16 and the pyrin-domain-only protein PYDC5 interfere with sensor and adaptor interactions, while TRIM11 limits AIM2 levels by promoting its degradation. The balance determines how much mature IL-1 family cytokine a DNA-exposed cell releases.

Microglia and astrocytes must be able to switch off an inflammatory response once a threat has passed, and dampening the neuroinflammatory response is what keeps immune activity in the brain from damaging the tissue it protects. Neurons signal their health directly to microglia through ligand-receptor pairs such as CD200-CD200R1 and fractalkine, holding resident phagocytes in a quiescent state; loss of this restraint gives synapse loss, chronic gliosis and progressive neurodegeneration. Other components act inside the microglial cell, where progranulin, TREM2 and cystatin F set the threshold and duration of activation, and mutations in progranulin or TREM2 cause frontotemporal dementia and raise Alzheimer risk. Anti-inflammatory cytokine and growth factor input, a circadian transcriptional repressor, and several microRNAs add further layers of suppression, linking immune tone in the CNS to lipid handling, sleep-wake timing and repair.

Not every amino acid a cell makes is destined for protein; this route covers synthesis of amino acids that act as neurotransmitters, metabolic intermediates or structural modifications. Glutamate decarboxylases GAD1 and GAD2 generate GABA, the principal inhibitory transmitter, and serine racemase produces D-serine, the co-agonist at NMDA receptors, tying this chemistry directly to synaptic excitability; loss of GABA synthesis provokes seizures. Other members feed ornithine and citrulline production for the urea cycle and carbamoyl phosphate synthesis, while procollagen lysyl hydroxylases create hydroxylysine residues needed for collagen crosslinking, and their deficiency causes a form of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. Transporters and catabolic enzymes such as ABAT and DPYD set the surrounding flux, so the pathway sits at the junction of nitrogen disposal, neurotransmission and extracellular matrix maturation.

Lactone metabolism covers the making and breaking of cyclic esters, and the genes here point to two concrete arms of it: paraoxonase-family lactonases and the handling of ascorbate, whose oxidised form dehydroascorbate is itself a lactone. PON1, PON2 and PON3 hydrolyse lactones and related esters, PON1 circulating in plasma in association with HDL and also able to hydrolyse organophosphate substrates, while PON2 acts intracellularly. Vitamin C enters cells either as ascorbate through the sodium-dependent transporters SLC23A1 and SLC23A2 or as dehydroascorbate through the glucose carriers SLC2A1 and SLC2A3, after which it must be reduced back to the active vitamin; glutathione supply via GCLC and thiol-active enzymes including GSTO1, GSTO2, ERO1A and SELENON tie this chemistry to cellular redox balance. The net result is antioxidant capacity, cofactor availability for collagen and catecholamine synthesis, and detoxification of reactive esters.</description>}Understanding the Ecological Relationship Between the Atlantic Puffin and the Sandeel: A Study in Trophic Dependency and Climate-Driven Mismatch

When DNA damage is too severe to repair, p53 can commit a cell to death through the mitochondrial arm of apoptosis, and this pathway covers the inputs that tune how readily that commitment happens. The balance matters in both directions: too little killing lets damaged cells persist and become tumorigenic, while too much destroys tissue after genotoxic stress or chemotherapy. Control acts at several levels. RPL26 binds p53 mRNA to boost its translation, while SIRT1 deacetylates p53 and dampens its output, and TAF9/TAF9B and HNRNPK support transactivation of target genes. ZNF385A biases p53 toward cell-cycle arrest genes such as p21 rather than apoptotic ones. At the mitochondrion, BCL2 and TRIAP1 restrain permeabilization and caspase-9 activation. Survival signals from CD44, MUC1, MIF and CD74 feed in, linking the decision to the cell's surface and inflammatory context.

Glutamate is the main excitatory transmitter in the brain, and tuning how much of it is released at a synapse sets the gain of excitatory transmission, shaping learning, cortical excitability and the threshold for excitotoxic damage. This regulatory layer acts at several points: STXBP1 (Munc18-1) primes and chaperones the SNARE machinery that fuses transmitter-filled vesicles with the presynaptic membrane, and RAB3GAP1 is the catalytic subunit of the Rab3 GTPase-activating complex, stimulating GTP hydrolysis on Rab3 during the vesicle cycle. Substrate supply matters too: the amino acid transporter SLC38A2 imports glutamine for conversion to glutamate, while KMO diverts tryptophan metabolism along the kynurenine route toward metabolites that modulate glutamate receptors. DTNBP1 links the process to presynaptic release regulation. Loss of STXBP1 causes severe early-onset epileptic encephalopathy, underscoring how narrowly release must be controlled.

When tissue is injured, the parenchyma that is lost can be replaced by fibrous connective tissue rather than by functional cells, and this pathway covers the controls that set how far that replacement goes. Tuning it decides whether a wound heals or progresses to fibrosis and scarring of the heart, lung, liver or kidney, where deposited matrix stiffens the organ and displaces its working tissue. The protein components act on myofibroblast behaviour and contractility: the Rho-dependent kinases ROCK1 and ROCK2 transmit cytoskeletal tension, calcineurin's catalytic subunit couples calcium signals to transcription, PPARG restrains fibrogenic activation, and RUNX1 and the advanced glycation end-product receptor AGER link inflammatory and metabolic stress to the same programme. A large share of the regulators here are microRNAs, including the miR-34 and miR-15/16 families, miR-17, miR-195, miR-199 and miR-214, which set matrix and growth-factor gene output post-transcriptionally.

When oxygen falls low enough that a cell cannot maintain its metabolism, the intrinsic apoptotic signalling pathway triggered by hypoxia decides whether that cell dies, committing it through mitochondrial permeabilisation and the execution phase of apoptosis rather than through an external death receptor. The genes involved illustrate both the death-promoting and the restraining sides of this decision. BNIP3, a BH3-only protein induced under low oxygen, acts at the mitochondrial outer membrane, while PINK1 links mitochondrial quality surveillance to survival, and NOL3 (ARC) and TMBIM6 oppose commitment by dampening caspase activation and buffering calcium release from the endoplasmic reticulum. Kinase and transcriptional components such as MAP2K1, PIK3CB and ATF2 set the balance between adaptive survival signalling and death, alongside stress-response and glycolytic proteins that mark the hypoxic state itself.

Cells hold potassium far above its external concentration, and potassium ion import across the plasma membrane is how that gradient is built and defended. It sets the resting membrane potential, underwrites excitability in neurons, cardiac and skeletal muscle, and drives secondary transport of nutrients and other ions; it also supports renal potassium handling and gastric acid secretion. The central machinery is the Na+/K+-ATPase, with multiple catalytic alpha and glycoprotein beta subunits and small FXYD regulatory partners that tune its pumping, alongside related gastric and non-gastric H+/K+-ATPases. Inward-rectifier channels of the KCNJ family, some coupled to sulfonylurea receptor subunits that link them to ATP levels, together with hyperpolarization-activated HCN channels, carry inward potassium flux, while NKCC-type cotransporters load potassium in epithelia. Mutations in these components cause cardiac arrhythmia, renal salt-wasting syndromes, deafness and neurological disease.

CXCL1 is a neutrophil-attracting chemokine, and this pathway covers the inputs that turn its production up in epithelial cells, fibroblasts and other tissue-resident cells. Raising CXCL1 output is how a tissue signals that neutrophils are needed, so the regulators here sit upstream of acute inflammatory cell recruitment rather than inside the chemokine's own signalling. The dominant input is IL-17 family cytokines: IL17A and IL17F acting through the IL17RA-containing receptor drive transcription of CXCL1 along with other neutrophil chemoattractants and antimicrobial products, a hallmark of type 17 immunity at mucosal and skin surfaces. TIRAP contributes as the adaptor that couples TLR2 and TLR4 to downstream kinases and NF-κB after microbial recognition. TRPV4, a mechano- and osmosensitive cation channel, links mechanical or barrier stress to the same chemokine response.

Cytotoxic CD8-positive alpha-beta T cells kill infected and transformed cells, so the brakes on their activation determine whether that killing stays proportionate. Damping this response protects healthy tissue from collateral destruction, limits autoimmunity, and sets the threshold for tolerance; the same restraint, co-opted within tumours or chronic infection, leaves cytotoxic cells functionally exhausted. The genes here act at several levels. Inhibitory surface ligands such as CD274 (PD-L1) and VSIR deliver co-inhibitory signals to responding T cells, and LILRB1 is an inhibitory receptor that recognises MHC class I. Intracellularly, SOCS1 shuts down cytokine receptor signalling through JAK-STAT, curbing the interleukin-driven amplification of effector responses. ZBTB7B instead operates developmentally, directing thymocyte lineage choice away from the CD8 fate toward CD4 helper cells. Together they place cytotoxic T cell activation under negative control at the ligand, cytokine and developmental levels.

Type I interferon alerts cells to viral infection, and the interferon alpha response is the transcriptional programme it switches on: genes up-regulated by alpha interferon that together put a cell into an antiviral state. Their products restrict viruses at nearly every step — RNA sensors such as IFIH1 and DHX58 detect viral nucleic acid, EIF2AK2 and the OAS enzymes shut down translation and trigger RNA degradation, MX1 and the IFITM proteins block entry and replication, and BST2 tethers budding virions. In parallel, elevated antigen presentation machinery, including TAP1 and the immunoproteasome subunits PSMB8 and PSMB9, and chemokines such as CXCL10 and CXCL11 recruit and arm lymphocytes. ISG15 conjugation, the STAT2–IRF9 transcription module and the deconjugating enzyme USP18 both propagate and restrain the signal, so much of the output is feedback control of interferon signalling itself.

Oxidative deamination of biogenic amines by the two monoamine oxidases, MAOA and MAOB, is the main route by which neurotransmitter and dietary amines are broken down. The reaction converts an amine to the corresponding aldehyde with reduction of oxygen to hydrogen peroxide; for primary amines such as serotonin or dopamine, ammonia is also released, while secondary and tertiary amines yield the shortened amine instead. Both are flavin-dependent enzymes anchored in the outer mitochondrial membrane, sharing over 70% sequence identity and many substrates, yet differing in preference: MAOA acts best on serotonin, MAOB on phenylethylamine, and their relative abundance differs between tissues such as fibroblasts and platelets. Because this step limits how long monoamines persist, the enzymes are longstanding drug targets, with inhibitors used as antidepressants and in Parkinson disease; loss of MAOA activity is linked to altered amine excretion and behaviour.

An integrated HIV-1 provirus makes new virus only by borrowing the host cell's own RNA polymerase II machinery, and transcription of the HIV genome is that borrowing. The long terminal repeat at the 5' end supplies promoter and enhancer sequences that recruit cellular transcription factors, so every viral protein ultimately depends on general host initiation and elongation components: TBP with its TAF partners, the TFIIA/TFIIB/TFIIE/TFIIF factors, TFIIH with its CDK7-cyclin H kinase module, and the P-TEFb subunits CDK9 and cyclin T1. Promoter-proximal pausing imposed by NELF and DSIF is the key control point; the viral Tat protein binds the TAR stem-loop in the nascent transcript and recruits P-TEFb to convert stalled polymerase into productive elongation, aided by elongation factors and the FACT histone chaperone. Capping enzymes and the nuclear cap-binding complex then process transcripts that serve as mRNAs, spliced templates for regulatory proteins, and packaged genomic RNA.

Growth-factor signalling through ERK must be switched off as well as on, and this is the step in which ERKs are inactivated by dephosphorylation. The activating mark on ERK1 and ERK2 (and the related ERK5) is a dual phosphothreonine-phosphotyrosine pair in the kinase activation loop; removing either one returns the kinase to its resting state, setting how long and how strongly a stimulus is read. Dual-specificity MAP kinase phosphatases such as DUSP6 and DUSP7, which prefer ERK, act in the cytoplasm and nucleus, while the serine/threonine phosphatase PP2A contributes through its catalytic, scaffolding and regulatory subunits; VRK3 acts as a scaffold promoting phosphatase action on ERK. Because active MAP kinases induce transcription of phosphatase genes, this arm forms a negative feedback loop that shapes signal duration and limits proliferative output.

Neurotrophin binding to the p75 neurotrophin receptor turns the receptor's cytoplasmic tail into a docking platform, and the complexes it recruits determine whether a neuron survives, grows, or dies. Because p75NTR has no catalytic activity of its own, everything depends on which adaptors arrive: here the assembly built around NGF-bound receptor gathers RIPK2, MYD88 and IRAK1 together with the scaffold p62 and atypical protein kinase C iota, converging on TRAF6. TRAF6 acts as an E3 ubiquitin ligase, and the polyubiquitin supplied by the ubiquitin genes in this module drives activation of the IKK complex through IKBKB, freeing NF-kB to enter the nucleus and switch on survival and inflammatory transcription. This arm of neurotrophin signalling opposes the pro-apoptotic outputs of the same receptor, and its balance shapes developmental neuronal pruning, axon growth and injury responses.

During pancreas development, a subset of ductal epithelial progenitors turns on NEUROG3 and is thereby committed to the endocrine lineage that gives rise to the islet cells producing insulin, glucagon, somatostatin and other hormones. The transcriptional programme run in these endocrine-committed progenitors converts that commitment into a differentiated hormone-secreting identity, so it sits upstream of glucose homeostasis and the endocrine, rather than acinar or ductal, fate. NEUROG3 itself directs transcription of a further set of regulators, including PAX4, NEUROD1, NKX2-2 and INSM1, which together specify islet subtypes and drive hormone gene expression and the maturation of secretory cells. Much of the evidence comes from mouse development, where the same factor dependencies are conserved. Because these factors act in a hierarchy, disruption at any level compromises islet formation and endocrine function.

One branch of epidermal growth factor receptor signalling converts ligand binding into a lipid second-messenger burst, and this is the step where EGFR interacts with phospholipase C-gamma. Any of the receptor's ligands -- EGF itself, transforming growth factor alpha, amphiregulin, epiregulin, epigen, betacellulin or heparin-binding EGF -- dimerises and autophosphorylates the receptor, creating phosphotyrosine docking sites. PLCG1 binds through its SH2 domains, is phosphorylated, and hydrolyses phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate at the inner face of the plasma membrane into inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate and diacylglycerol. IP3 releases calcium from intracellular stores, while diacylglycerol remains in the membrane and activates protein kinase C. The pathway therefore links a receptor tyrosine kinase to phosphoinositide turnover and calcium mobilisation, distinct from the MAPK and PI3K routes that the same receptor also engages.

Cytosolic isocitrate dehydrogenase 1 normally oxidises isocitrate to 2-oxoglutarate while reducing NADP+, supplying NADPH for cytosolic reductive biosynthesis and antioxidant defence. Somatic mutations at arginine 132, found at high frequency in glioblastoma and other tumours, convert the enzyme into one that instead reduces 2-oxoglutarate with NADPH to 2-hydroxyglutarate, so that cells expressing the mutant accumulate elevated levels of this metabolite in the cytosol. This abnormal conversion is a gain of a new catalytic activity rather than simple loss of function, and the mutation is heterozygous, leaving one wild-type subunit. 2-Hydroxyglutarate closely resembles 2-oxoglutarate and can interfere with dioxygenases that use it as cosubstrate, notably histone and DNA demethylases, contributing to the hypermethylated, differentiation-blocked phenotype of these tumours. The metabolite's ultimate fate is unclear, but its consistent appearance in primary tumours suggests it favours tumour cell growth, and it serves as a diagnostic marker and drug target.

Every round of protein synthesis in the cytoplasm begins with charging a tRNA with its matching amino acid, and cytosolic tRNA aminoacylation is the step that establishes the genetic code physically: each synthetase reads both an amino acid and the tRNAs that carry its codons, joining them using ATP and releasing AMP and pyrophosphate. Errors or shortfalls here limit translation capacity and can introduce the wrong residue into nascent chains. The enzymes here cover the standard amino acids, with a bifunctional glutamyl-prolyl enzyme and a two-subunit phenylalanyl enzyme; eight of them assemble with the accessory proteins AIMP1, AIMP2 and EEF1E1 into a multi-synthetase complex thought to channel charged tRNAs efficiently to elongating ribosomes. Several members also have signalling roles outside translation, and inherited mutations in individual synthetases, including GARS1 and AARS1, cause peripheral neuropathy.

Leukocytes find their way to infection, injury and lymphoid tissue by reading gradients of secreted chemoattractant proteins, and the binding of chemokines to their G protein-coupled receptors is the recognition step that sets that migration in motion. Ligands of the CC, CXC, CX3C and XC families engage matching receptors such as CCR1-CCR10, CXCR1-CXCR6, CX3CR1 and XCR1, triggering calcium flux, integrin activation and directed chemotaxis. The pairings define immune cell behaviour: CCR7 with CCL19 and CCL21 routes dendritic cells and naive T cells into lymph nodes, CXCR4 with CXCL12 retains progenitors in bone marrow, and CXCR1/CXCR2 with CXCL8 recruits neutrophils to inflamed tissue. Atypical receptors including ACKR2, ACKR3 and ACKR4 bind ligands without conventional signalling, scavenging them to shape gradients. This signalling underlies inflammation, lymphoid organisation, HIV entry and tumour metastasis.

Dolichol kinase converts dolichol to dolichyl phosphate in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, the lipid carrier on which the oligosaccharide precursor for N-linked glycosylation is built and which also supplies O-mannosylation and GPI anchor synthesis. When DOLK activity is lost, dolichyl phosphate becomes limiting and glycan transfer to nascent proteins fails across many substrates at once, producing the underglycosylated serum glycoproteins that define a type I congenital disorder of glycosylation. The resulting DOLK-CDG is a severe multisystem disease, with dilated cardiomyopathy, ichthyosis, seizures, hypotonia and developmental failure, and death frequently occurs in infancy. Because the affected step sits upstream of all dolichol-dependent glycosylation rather than within one glycan branch, the defect illustrates how a single lipid-activating kinase governs secretory protein maturation, membrane protein folding and cell surface anchoring throughout the body.

Death receptor signalling can end in apoptosis or in regulated necrosis, and blocking caspase-8 proteolytic activity is what tips the decision toward the necrotic route. Fully processed caspase-8 not only drives the apoptotic cascade but also cleaves RIPK1 and RIPK3, thereby restraining the kinase-dependent necroptotic programme; when its activity is suppressed, those kinases survive intact and signal necrosis instead. Ligands such as FASLG and TRAIL engage FAS and the TRAIL receptors TNFRSF10A/B, which recruit FADD to assemble a platform where procaspase-8 dimerises, with TRADD and TRAF2 serving as adaptors in the related tumour necrosis factor receptor complexes. Inhibition arises from cellular FLIP encoded by CFLAR, from viral FLIP-like proteins, or from pharmacological pan-caspase inhibitors, each converting a silent apoptotic outcome into membrane rupture and release of cell contents.

CFTR is a cAMP-regulated chloride channel in the apical membrane of epithelia, and the chloride and bicarbonate it moves set the hydration and pH of airway, pancreatic, intestinal and biliary secretions. When mutation prevents the protein from folding, as with the common F508del allele, the channel never reaches the surface and cystic fibrosis follows: thick unclearable mucus and chronic lung infection, exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, meconium ileus, biliary disease, salty sweat and male infertility. The genes here trace the fate of the misfolded protein rather than the channel's transport function — lectin-like ER quality control and retention factors such as OS9, ERLEC1 and the SEL1L complex, membrane ubiquitin ligases RNF5 and RNF185, the VCP ATPase and derlin channels that retrotranslocate the substrate, and the ubiquitin and 26S proteasome machinery that degrades it. Loss of function is thus a disposal problem imposed by endoplasmic-reticulum-associated degradation.

Newborn lungs cannot inflate without pulmonary surfactant, and the lipid transporter ABCA3 is what loads the lipids that make it. Sitting in the limiting membrane of lamellar bodies in alveolar type II cells, ABCA3 moves phospholipids and cholesterol into these storage organelles, where they are assembled with surfactant proteins into bilayer membranes that are secreted and spread as a surface film at the air-liquid interface, lowering surface tension so alveoli stay open. When ABCA3 is defective, this fails: normal lamellar bodies are absent, small vesicular structures carry electron-dense inclusions, and surfactant lipid is not secreted, so lipoproteinaceous material accumulates in the alveolar space. The result is pulmonary surfactant metabolism dysfunction type 3, a usually fatal neonatal respiratory distress. The biology links ABC-transporter-driven lipid translocation to lysosome-related organelle biogenesis and to lung development.

The mitotic cell cycle is the ordered programme by which a cell duplicates its genome and partitions it equally into two daughters, passing through G1, S, G2 and M with quiescence as an alternative exit. Its fidelity determines tissue growth and renewal, and its deregulation through cyclin, CDK inhibitor and retinoblastoma-pathway lesions is a hallmark of cancer. Cyclin-dependent kinases paired with D, E, A and B cyclins drive the transitions, restrained by CDK inhibitors, WEE1 and phosphatases and reset by ubiquitin-mediated proteolysis through SCF and the anaphase-promoting complex with the proteasome. Origin licensing on ORC and MCM proteins commits cells to replication; centrosome maturation, gamma-tubulin nucleation, kinetochore assembly, cohesin and condensin, spindle checkpoint surveillance, nuclear envelope and Golgi breakdown, and ESCRT-dependent abscission complete division.</description>}

Newly transcribed tRNAs are not usable until they are trimmed, spliced, tailed, modified and delivered to the cytosol, and tRNA processing covers that whole maturation route in both the nucleus and the mitochondrial matrix. Accurate translation depends on it: anticodon and wobble modifications set decoding fidelity, and defects cause microcephaly, intellectual disability, sideroblastic anaemia with immunodeficiency, pontocerebellar hypoplasia and mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, while variants near CDKAL1 are linked to type 2 diabetes through impaired insulin production. RNase P complexes remove 5' leaders, ELAC2 cleaves 3' trailers, TRNT1 adds the untemplated CCA end, and the TSEN endonuclease with RTCB-containing ligase excises introns and rejoins exons. A large modification enzyme set writes methyl, pseudouridine, thiol, queuosine, wybutosine and threonylcarbamoyl marks. Nucleoporins and the exportin XPOT handle nuclear export, and mitochondrial transcripts are excised from polycistronic precursors alongside the rRNAs and mRNAs they flank.

Ribosomes cannot be built until their RNA components are carved out of a long precursor and chemically decorated, and rRNA processing is that work. A single 47S transcript made by RNA polymerase I in the nucleolus is cleaved by endonucleases and trimmed by exonucleases to yield 18S rRNA for the small subunit and 5.8S and 28S rRNA for the large subunit, while ribosomal proteins of the RPS and RPL families assemble onto the maturing particles. Helicases, the UTP-containing small subunit processome, the RNA exosome with its nuclear helicase partner, and XRN2 carry out cleavage and degradation of discarded spacers; guide snoRNPs containing dyskerin, GAR1 and NOP10 direct pseudouridylation, and methyltransferases such as fibrillarin add 2'-O-methyl and base modifications. A parallel set of enzymes processes and modifies the mitochondrial 12S and 16S rRNAs cut from the polycistronic mitochondrial transcript. Defects in ribosome biogenesis factors cause human disease.

Translation converts mRNA sequence into polypeptide, and this collection covers the whole of it: initiation, elongation and termination on cytosolic ribosomes, the parallel machinery of the mitochondrion, the routing of secretory proteins into the endoplasmic reticulum, and the quality control that clears failed products. Large and small subunit ribosomal proteins provide the catalytic platform; aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases charge tRNAs, with separate cytosolic and mitochondrial enzymes; eIF3, eIF4F and eIF2 complexes assemble the start site and are the point where growth signals and stress restrain protein output. Nascent hydrophobic signal sequences are captured by the signal recognition particle, delivered to its ER receptor and threaded through the Sec61 translocon before signal peptidase cleavage. Inside mitochondria, mitoribosomes translate the thirteen respiratory chain subunits encoded by mtDNA and insert them cotranslationally via OXA1L. Stalled ribosomes are resolved by rescue and ubiquitin-proteasome factors including PELO, ZNF598 and LTN1.

Adenosine-to-inosine conversion is the most common form of mRNA editing in humans, rewriting transcripts after they are made so that a single gene can yield proteins of different function. Because the translation machinery reads inosine as guanosine, editing can change codons and therefore amino acids, and it is especially prevalent in the brain, where it tunes the properties of ion channels and neurotransmitter receptors. The deaminases ADAR and ADARB1 carry out the reaction, each combining double-stranded RNA binding domains with a catalytic deaminase domain and recognising structural features of pre-mRNA rather than a linear sequence motif. Well-characterised targets include the Q/R site of the AMPA receptor GluR2 subunit, whose editing renders the heteromeric receptor impermeable to calcium, and serotonin 5-HT2C receptor mRNA, where editing yields isoforms with reduced G-protein coupling. Editing of duplex RNA also shapes how the cell distinguishes its own transcripts from foreign ones.

Before any collagen can leave the cell, three polypeptide chains must find each other and lock together in correct register, and collagen chain trimerization is that first assembly step. It sets the composition of each molecule -- homotrimer or specific heterotrimer -- which in turn dictates whether the product becomes a fibril, a basement membrane network, a beaded filament, or an anchoring structure. In the fibrillar collagens the C-propeptides drive this recognition, selecting partner chains, aligning them, and nucleating triple helix formation at the C-terminus so that folding then propagates toward the N-terminus in zipper-like fashion; in type III a C-terminal disulfide linkage holds the chains together permanently. Other members of the family, including the transmembrane and several non-fibrillar collagens, use different domains to oligomerize. The genes span essentially the whole collagen family, and correct chain selection here is a prerequisite for secretion and extracellular matrix assembly.

Rather than build every nucleotide from scratch, cells recover the nucleosides and free bases released by RNA and DNA turnover and rephosphorylate them to monophosphates, feeding them back into nucleotide biosynthesis and interconversion. This recycling is energetically cheaper than de novo synthesis and is the route by which resting cells, and tissues such as brain that synthesise purines poorly, maintain their nucleotide pools; deoxyribonucleotide salvage runs at a low level because DNA turnover is limited. Phosphoribosyltransferases act on purine bases while kinases such as ADK, DCK, DGUOK, TK1, TK2 and the uridine-cytidine kinases handle nucleosides, with phosphorylases and deaminases channelling bases between purine and pyrimidine routes. Loss of HPRT1 causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome with hyperuricaemia and severe neurological disease; adenosine deaminase deficiency causes immunodeficiency, and mutations in the mitochondrial kinases TK2 and DGUOK deplete mitochondrial DNA. The same enzymes activate nucleoside analogue drugs.

Dietary fat absorbed by the small intestine cannot travel through blood or lymph unless it is packaged, and chylomicron assembly is the enterocyte process that builds those packages. Each nascent particle nucleates on a single molecule of apolipoprotein B-48, onto which microsomal triglyceride transfer protein — a heterodimer with protein disulfide isomerase — loads triacylglycerol, phospholipid and cholesterol as the apolipoprotein is translocated into the endoplasmic reticulum lumen. Exchangeable apolipoproteins A-I, A-II and A-IV join the surface, with apoC-II, apoC-III and apoE added or acquired to control later lipolysis by lipoprotein lipase and hepatic clearance of remnants. The particle then leaves the ER in specialized vesicles requiring the COPII component SAR1B before secretion into lymph. Loss of the transfer protein causes abetalipoproteinemia, and SAR1B defects cause chylomicron retention disease, both producing fat malabsorption and deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins.

Inflammation does not simply fade; it is actively switched off by short-lived lipid signals, and the omega-3 fatty acid DPAn-3 is one of the substrates from which those signals are made. Sitting as an intermediate between EPA and DHA, DPAn-3 is also converted into its own family of specialised proresolving mediators, counterparts of the DHA-derived resolvins, protectins and maresins, that limit neutrophil recruitment and promote macrophage clearance of debris. Oxygenation is carried out by the lipoxygenases ALOX5, ALOX12 and ALOX15, which insert molecular oxygen at defined positions to give hydroperoxy intermediates that are further converted to epoxides, diols and trihydroxy products; cyclooxygenase-2 contributes an aspirin-sensitive route to related mediators. The pathway links dietary omega-3 intake to the resolution phase of the innate immune response rather than to prostaglandin-type pro-inflammatory signalling.

Meiotic recombination is how homologous chromosomes exchange DNA during gamete formation, shuffling alleles between parental chromosomes and, just as importantly, physically tethering each homolog pair so that the first meiotic division segregates them correctly. Without at least one crossover per bivalent, chromosomes missegregate, producing aneuploid eggs and sperm, infertility and pregnancy loss. The process begins with programmed double-strand breaks made by SPO11, whose covalent attachment to the DNA is removed nucleolytically before the MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex and its partner RBBP8 resect the ends. RPA-coated 3' overhangs are handed to the RecA-like strand exchange proteins RAD51 and DMC1, aided by MND1 and PSMC3IP, which invade the homolog. Most intermediates resolve without crossover; a minority mature through MSH4-MSH5 and MLH1-MLH3 into chiasmata. PRDM9 marks hotspots by methylating histones, targeting breaks to defined genomic positions.

Oxidative attack on DNA leaves lesions that must be excised before they block replication or cause mutation, and the glycosylase NEIL3 is the enzyme that initiates that removal in a particular niche: single-stranded DNA, telomeric repeats, and replication forks. It cleaves hydantoin products of guanine oxidation and thymine glycol, and also unhooks certain interstrand crosslinks independently of the Fanconi anaemia route, so loss of activity leaves both oxidative base damage and crosslinks unresolved. Failure of this arm of base excision repair has consequences beyond mutagenesis: an inactivating variant predisposes to autoimmune disease, depletion accelerates telomere loss, and deficiency limits proliferation of neural stem cells and adult hippocampal neurogenesis, with learning and memory deficits. Expression rises in failing heart and atherosclerotic plaque, where its protective role appears only partly explained by DNA repair.

Maturation of the SARS-CoV-2 envelope (E) protein covers the post-translational modifications that convert the newly translated viral protein into its functional, membrane-associated form. E is a small hydrophobic protein that accumulates in the endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi and ERGIC membranes, where it contributes to virion assembly, budding and the ion-channel (porin-like) activity attributed to E trimers rather than trafficking to the plasma membrane. After synthesis the protein is palmitoylated on cysteines, which stabilises its membrane interaction, and is ubiquitinated using the host ubiquitin pool supplied by the ribosomal fusion precursors and polyubiquitin genes represented here. Because correctly matured E is required for efficient production of infectious particles and for the membrane remodelling that accompanies coronaviral egress, this step links host protein-modification machinery to the late stages of the viral replication cycle and to candidate antiviral targets.

Internal tandem duplication of the receptor tyrosine kinase FLT3 is one of the most common lesions in acute myeloid leukaemia, and one reason it drives disease is that the mutant receptor engages STAT5 far more strongly than wild-type FLT3 or kinase-domain mutants do. Constitutively active FLT3 ITD, retained in intracellular compartments and signalling aberrantly, recruits the adaptors GRB2 and GAB2 together with the phosphatase PTPN11 (SHP2), leading to phosphorylation and nuclear translocation of STAT5A and STAT5B. The transcriptional output includes the anti-apoptotic BCL2L1, the kinase PIM1, CDKN1A and the NADPH oxidase NOX4, whose reactive oxygen species feed back on phosphatase activity. The net effect is myeloid progenitor survival, altered cell cycle control and resistance to apoptosis, which makes this axis a determinant of prognosis and a target of FLT3 kinase inhibitors.

RHOBTB3 looks like a small GTPase but behaves differently: its divergent Ras-like domain hydrolyses ATP rather than GTP, so its nucleotide cycle is an ATPase cycle. The protein works at the interface of membrane traffic and protein turnover, and it matters because retrograde delivery of cargo from endosomes back to the Golgi depends on it, in cooperation with RAB9 and endosomal sorting machinery such as HGS. Beyond the GTPase-like domain, tandem BTB domains and a BACK domain let RHOBTB3 serve as a substrate-recruiting adaptor for CUL3-based ubiquitin ligases, linking it to regulated proteolysis; a C-terminal prenylation motif anchors it to membranes. It is broadly expressed and has been implicated in cell cycle regulation and in the adaptive response to hypoxia. Expression falls in many tumour types, which has prompted proposals that it acts as a tumour suppressor.

Late in infection by enveloped viruses, the same fusion machinery that mediates viral entry can act between neighbouring cells, merging them into multinucleated syncytia. Induction of cell-cell fusion of this kind is a hallmark of severe COVID-19 lung pathology, where infected syncytial pneumocytes are found, and it is thought to help the virus spread without exposing particles to antibodies; such syncytia can also engulf and destroy lymphocytes, a possible contributor to lymphopenia. Mechanistically, coronavirus spike on one cell engages ACE2 on another, forming synapse-like contacts from finger-like projections that progress to a fusion pore and full membrane merger. Proteolytic priming of spike by the cell surface protease TMPRSS2 and by furin, which cleaves spike into S1 and S2, raises fusion efficiency, and several variants show enhanced syncytium formation. Anoctamin family membrane proteins are implicated alongside these components.

Adipogenesis is the developmental programme that turns mesenchymal precursors into fat cells, the main cellular constituent of adipose tissue and a central node in whole-body energy balance. White adipocytes store and release fatty acids on demand, while brown and the beige cells induced within white depots dissipate energy as heat; genes such as UCP1, CIDEA, DIO2 and ELOVL3 mark the thermogenic arm, and PRDM16 with EBF2 and PPARGC1A specify it. Commitment runs through a transcriptional cascade in which CEBPB and CEBPD precede CEBPA and the master regulator PPARG acting with RXRA, driving lipid handling and endocrine output including LPL, CD36, FABP4, PLIN1, ADIPOQ and LEP. Much of the set is coregulatory machinery: the full Mediator complex, p300/CBP and NCOA coactivators, NCOR1/2 and HDAC-containing corepressors, and NuRD subunits, which convert TGF-beta/BMP, WNT and inflammatory inputs into chromatin-level decisions about adipocyte identity.

Cells continuously read the physical forces around them — blood flow shear stress, mechanical load, stretch, touch — and convert them into chemical signals, the process captured here as cellular responses to mechanical stimuli. This is how endothelium adapts to laminar versus turbulent flow, how osteocytes sense load and fluid flow, and how specialized touch structures such as Merkel cells and Pacinian corpuscles report contact. Force is detected by mechanically gated channels including PIEZO1 and TRPV4, by integrins bound to fibronectin and their adhesion plaque partners talin, vinculin and focal adhesion kinase, and by junctional and receptor proteins such as PECAM1, VE-cadherin and the adrenomedullin receptor components. Downstream, heterotrimeric G proteins and adenylate cyclases, PI3K–AKT–mTOR, calcium channels and calpains, NF-κB subunits, eNOS, purinergic signalling through pannexin and P2 receptors, and the transcriptional coactivator YAP1 amplify the signal into altered gene expression, nitric oxide production, growth and cell behaviour.

Dengue virus carries a small genome and must borrow host machinery to replicate and to blunt the response against it; these virus-host interactions describe where its proteins go in an infected cell and what they bind. The consequences are clinical: secreted NS1 circulates, enters uninfected cells and, together with nuclear NS5, engages junctional proteins such as ZO-1 and triggers matrix metalloproteinase activity, driving the vascular leak of dengue hemorrhagic fever. Immune evasion runs through the innate sensing arm represented here by cGAS, STING, MAVS, IFIH1, TRIM25 and STAT2, while receptors including CLEC5A and TLR4 with LY96 and complement components shape inflammation. A large share of the interactors are nuclear RNA-processing factors — spliceosomal snRNPs, SF3 and PRPF subunits, hnRNPs, SR proteins, cleavage and polyadenylation factors and RNA polymerase II — alongside autophagy initiation, mTOR complex components and heparan sulfate proteoglycans used at entry.

Antibodies gain their high affinity after an immune response begins, and affinity selection of immunoglobulins is the germinal centre process that does the choosing. In the light zone of a germinal centre, B cells test their receptors against antigen held as immune complexes on follicular dendritic cells through FCGR2B and the complement receptors CR1 and CR2; high-affinity clones extract antigen-bearing membrane using non-muscle myosin IIA and the actin cytoskeleton. Internalised antigen is degraded by cathepsins and presented on MHC class II to T follicular helper cells, whose CD40L, IL4 and IL21 signals block apoptosis and license return to the dark zone. There, AICDA-driven somatic hypermutation, error-prone polymerases and mismatch repair diversify the immunoglobulin variable regions, supported by transcription elongation and chromatin remodelling machinery, and the cycle of mutation and selection repeats. Transcription factors including BCL6, PAX5, IRF4 and PRDM1 set the germinal centre state and its exit.
